enonce_markdown: A porter in a Douala market lifts a sack of maize of mass $25\,\mathrm{kg}$ from the ground onto a lorry platform $1.2\,\mathrm{m}$ high. Taking $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the work done by the porter against gravity is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The work done in lifting a load at steady speed is the force needed (its weight $mg$) multiplied by the vertical distance moved: $W = mgh$.

### Solution

Weight of the sack: $mg = 25 \times 10 = 250\,\mathrm{N}$.

$W = mgh = 250 \times 1.2 = 300\,\mathrm{J}$.

The value $30\,\mathrm{J}$ forgets $g$ ($25 \times 1.2$). The value $250$ is only the weight in newtons, not a work in joules. The value $3\,000\,\mathrm{J}$ is a power-of-ten slip. **Answer: c.**

enonce_markdown: An electric water pump in a Bamenda compound does $4\,800\,\mathrm{J}$ of work in $1$ minute. Its power is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Power is the work done (or energy transferred) per unit time: $P = \dfrac{W}{t}$. The time must be in seconds so that the power comes out in watts ($1\,\mathrm{W} = 1\,\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$).

### Solution

$t = 1\ \text{minute} = 60\,\mathrm{s}$.

$P = \dfrac{W}{t} = \dfrac{4\,800}{60} = 80\,\mathrm{W}$.

$4\,800\,\mathrm{W}$ comes from dividing by the number $1$ of minutes without converting; $288\,000\,\mathrm{W}$ comes from multiplying by $60$ instead of dividing; $8\,\mathrm{W}$ is a decimal slip. **Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown: A small trolley of mass $0.2\,\mathrm{kg}$ is released from rest at the top of a smooth (frictionless) curved track. The top of the track is $0.8\,\mathrm{m}$ above the bottom. Taking $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the speed of the trolley at the bottom is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

With no friction, the energy is conserved: the gravitational potential energy lost equals the kinetic energy gained, $mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$. The mass cancels.

### Solution

Energy lost: $mgh = 0.2 \times 10 \times 0.8 = 1.6\,\mathrm{J}$.

$\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.2 \times v^{2} = 1.6 \Rightarrow v^{2} = 16 \Rightarrow v = 4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

$2.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is $\sqrt{gh}$ (the factor $2$ is forgotten); $16$ is $v^{2}$ (the square root is forgotten); $8$ is $v^{2}/2$. **Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown: A hoist driven by an electric motor takes $2\,000\,\mathrm{W}$ of electrical power. It raises a load of $150\,\mathrm{kg}$ through a height of $8\,\mathrm{m}$ in $10\,\mathrm{s}$. Taking $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the efficiency of the hoist is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{useful power (or energy) output}}{\text{power (or energy) input}} \times 100\%$. The useful output here is the work done in lifting the load, divided by the time.

### Solution

Useful work: $W = mgh = 150 \times 10 \times 8 = 12\,000\,\mathrm{J}$.

Useful power: $P = \dfrac{12\,000}{10} = 1\,200\,\mathrm{W}$.

Efficiency $= \dfrac{1\,200}{2\,000} \times 100 = 60\%$.

$40\%$ is the percentage of energy wasted; $167\%$ comes from inverting the ratio (an efficiency can never exceed $100\%$); $6\%$ comes from forgetting $g$. **Answer: c.**

enonce_markdown:
A pump at a village borehole in Bafoussam raises $600\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water every minute from a depth of $15\,\mathrm{m}$ and delivers it at ground level at a negligible speed. Take $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

(i) Calculate the work done by the pump each minute. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Calculate the useful power of the pump. *[2 marks]*

(iii) The motor driving the pump is $75\%$ efficient. Calculate the electrical power it takes in. *[2 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Work done in raising a mass is $W = mgh$; power is $P = W/t$ with $t$ in seconds; and efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{useful output}}{\text{input}}$, so $\text{input} = \dfrac{\text{useful output}}{\text{efficiency}}$.

### Solution

(i) $W = mgh = 600 \times 10 \times 15 = 90\,000\,\mathrm{J}$ (in one minute).

(ii) $t = 60\,\mathrm{s}$, so $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = \dfrac{90\,000}{60} = 1\,500\,\mathrm{W}$.

(iii) Efficiency $= 0.75$, so input power $= \dfrac{1\,500}{0.75} = 2\,000\,\mathrm{W}$. The other $500\,\mathrm{W}$ is wasted as heat and sound in the motor.

enonce_markdown:
A car of mass $1\,000\,\mathrm{kg}$ travels at $20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ along a straight level road. The driver brakes and the car stops under a constant braking force of $4\,000\,\mathrm{N}$. Ignore air resistance.

(i) Calculate the kinetic energy of the car before braking. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Use the work done by the braking force to calculate the distance travelled before the car stops. *[2 marks]*

(iii) The same car, with the same braking force, is now travelling at $30\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Calculate its stopping distance, and explain why the distance is more than $1.5$ times the first one. *[3 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The work done by the braking force removes the kinetic energy of the car: $F \times d = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$. The kinetic energy depends on $v^{2}$.

### Solution

(i) $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1\,000 \times 20^{2} = 200\,000\,\mathrm{J}$.

(ii) Work done by the brakes $= Fd = E_k$, so $d = \dfrac{200\,000}{4\,000} = 50\,\mathrm{m}$.

(iii) At $30\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$: $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1\,000 \times 30^{2} = 450\,000\,\mathrm{J}$, so $d = \dfrac{450\,000}{4\,000} = 112.5\,\mathrm{m}$.

The speed has increased by a factor $1.5$, but the kinetic energy is proportional to $v^{2}$, so it increases by $1.5^{2} = 2.25$. For the same braking force, the stopping distance (proportional to the kinetic energy) is also multiplied by $2.25$: $50 \times 2.25 = 112.5\,\mathrm{m}$.
